units.translation: The high place, on which the many altars of the Tegeans are, is called the altar of Zeus Clarius, and it is clear that the surname was given to the god because of the allotment of the sons of Arcas.
we will bury him without lamentations
and these words are the beginning of lamentations
and to exchange a lamentable, hateful path of the house for freshly cut ones

That the ancient Attics used this spelling, not κλαίω [I weep], is attested by Apollonius on adverbs p. 600, 27: τὸ κλάω παρὰ Ἀττικοῖς ἐν μακρῷ τῷ α [the form κλάω among the Attics with long alpha], and other grammarians cited in the Thesaurus vol. 4 p. 1598. But the copyists, accustomed to the Homeric reading, generally introduced the diphthong. The examples in Aeschylus are nine or ten, if καλλίων [more beautiful] in fr. 135 was rightly changed to κλαίων [weeping] by Dobree: in all of which κλαίω [I weep] is written (except that κλάοις [you would weep] is preserved in M Suppl. 925), changed by me to the Attic form, with Porson and Elmsley leading the way, and likewise in the plays of Sophocles and Euripides. However, in the epic imperfect form fr. 298 (in Athenaeus 11 p. 491a) αἱ δ᾽ ἕπτ᾽ ῎Ατλαντος παῖδες ὠνομασμέναι κλαίεσκον [the seven daughters of Atlas, named, kept weeping] I retained the diphthong and did not write κλάεσκον [they kept weeping], because the matter is uncertain. But frequent examples of the correct spelling are in the manuscripts of Aristophanes, Plato, and other Attic writers. The same must be said of other words of this kind, such as κάω [I burn], ἐλάα [olive], ἀεί [always], which also are written in manuscripts sometimes in this way, sometimes with the diphthong.
it is not fitting to weep or lament
shall I weep for the childless war-chiefs?
how shall I dare not to weep for you?
I weep then, groaning for the misfortune of this house
weeping for the torch-bearings around you
you would weep, if you touched
and I utter words over things lamented
and I see this nurse of Orestes lamenting
the ashes of a man well lamented are hidden
the form κλάω among the Attics with long alpha
the seven daughters of Atlas, named, kept weeping
the famous wife of Zeus, about to be
he found vengeance for famous Athens
the quickly dying, woman-voiced report is destroyed
truly we have heard your prophetic fame
trampling on the fame of the future
and to the one who toils, from the gods is owed the offspring of his toil, fame
but the fame of the dead is alive
he stole the light of all-crafty fire and gave it to mortals
he could not deceive a mind that has eyes
I mean the thief of fire
